html:
Aksum was a trading kingdom in the highlands of what is now Eritrea and northern Ethiopia, from about the 1st century CE to the 10th. At its height it controlled the Red Sea trade between the Roman world and India and ruled parts of southern Arabia.

The Persian prophet Mani, in the 3rd century, named it one of the four great powers of the world, alongside Rome, Persia and China. Its port of Adulis shipped ivory, gold, incense and exotic animals, and took in goods from Egypt, Arabia and India.

What it left:

  • Coins. From about 270 it minted its own coins in gold, silver and bronze, one of very few states of the time to do so. They have been found as far away as India.
  • Stelae. Giant carved granite stelae marked royal tombs. The tallest still standing, the Obelisk of Axum, was taken to Rome by Mussolini and returned in 2005.
  • Ge'ez. Its language and script became the classical language of the Ethiopian church.
  • Christianity. King Ezana adopted Christianity in the mid-4th century, making Aksum one of the first Christian states. His coins switched from the crescent and disc to the cross.

Aksum fought for control of Yemen against the Himyarite Kingdom, and in the 520s King Kaleb invaded to protect Christians there. It also crushed what was left of Kush around 350.

In 613 to 615 its king sheltered the early Muslims who fled Mecca, the First Hijra. The rise of Islam and the Persian and then Arab control of the Red Sea cut its trade, and Aksum declined. Its heirs, from the Zagwe kings to the Ethiopian Empire, claimed its legacy.
